  `alloc` and re-materializes the slot as `&'static mut MaybeUninit<T>`; same rationale.
  `ensures` adds the `size_of::<T>()`/`align_of::<T>()` vs `(N, A)` guard arms.

## `external_body` introduced while speccing `arch::x86::mem::paging::table`

- `src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/paging/table.rs::Table::<E>::read` — reads a `TableEntry` from a
  page-table slot through a raw pointer materialized from `self.base` (`usize as *const E::Word`).
  Verus does not support `usize`→pointer casts (int-to-ptr materialization of externally-owned,
  volatile page-table memory), so the body cannot be verified. Same trust-boundary rationale as
  `bump_allocator::alloc` (`usize as *mut`) and `frame::instance`. See
  `nanvix-phys-arch-paging-table/verus-unsupported.md`. **The function is not contract-free:** it
  carries a full `#[verus_spec]` pinned to the global page-table-memory ghost — `requires index@ <
  PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`, `ensures result == spec_table_read::<E>(self@.addr, index@)` — exactly as
  `frame::instance` pins its result to `phys_view()` (parameter-free global ghost, no signature
  change).
- `src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/paging/table.rs::Table::<E>::write` — writes a `TableEntry` into a
  page-table slot through a raw pointer materialized from `self.base` (`usize as *mut E::Word`).
  Same int-to-ptr / volatile externally-owned-memory limitation as `read`. Carries only the sound
  `requires index@ < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH` (auto from `TableIndex::inv`); it has **no** contents
  `ensures`. A contents postcondition pinning the *pure* global ghost `spec_table_word(self@.addr,
  index@)` to the caller-chosen `entry` would be unsound for an `external_body` (assumed)
  contract: two writes of distinct entries to the same slot would assume
  `spec_entry_raw(e1) == spec_entry_raw(e2)`, which with `lemma_entry_roundtrip` derives
  `e1 == e2`, i.e. `false` (Turn 2 review #2/#3/#15; exploit reproduced). The genuine `old@ -> @`
  slot-update transition (`self@.entries[index@] == Some(entry)`, other slots framed) is therefore
  **deferred to the proving-phase page-table permission token**, exactly the `identity_map_view()`
  `v -> v'` deferral convention in `identity_map.spec.rs`.

## `external_body` introduced while speccing `arch::x86::mem::paging` (`mod.rs`)

- `src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/paging/mod.rs::invlpg` — the body is a single
  `core::arch::asm!` block issuing the `invlpg` instruction, which flushes the CPU TLB
  entry for `vaddr`. Verus does not support inline-asm expressions, so the body cannot be
  verified — an external-bottom hardware trust boundary (same class as the volatile
  page-table access in `table::read`/`write` and the int-to-pointer materialization in
  `frame::instance`/`bump_allocator::alloc`). See
  `nanvix-phys-arch-paging-mod/verus-unsupported.md`. The effect is purely on hardware TLB
  state (outside Verus' memory model and invisible to every caller's Rust-visible state),
  so the faithful contract is **empty**: no `requires` (any `usize` is accepted), trivial
  `ensures` (returns `()`, no Rust-visible effect, every caller-side invariant preserved).
  This matches the inherited upstream
  `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.spec.rs:151`
  `pub assume_specification[ ::arch::mem::paging::invlpg ](vaddr: usize);` (no
  `requires`/`ensures`). No exec signature changed.

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::get_mut`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::init`

## `external_body` introduced while speccing `mm::phys`

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/mod.rs::book_physical_memory_regions` — iterates an
  `alloc::collections::LinkedList` in a `for` loop. Verus has no `LinkedList` model and the
  orphan rule blocks providing one from the kernel crate (see
  `nanvix-phys-phys-mod/bugs.md`). Body cannot be verified; `ensures` states that, on `Ok`,
  every frame in `phys_regions_frame_set(&physical_memory_regions)` becomes reserved.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/mod.rs::book_mmio_regions` — same `LinkedList` limitation.

  becomes reserved (uncovered MMIO frames are skipped, matching the `frame::is_covered` gate).

# Bugs — `mm::phys::kframe`

No correctness/logic bugs found in the in-scope functions
(`KernelFrame::new`, `KernelFrame::base`, `KernelFrame::drop`).

## Build-hygiene fix (auto-fixed) — duplicate import (kframe.rs)

**What**: `kframe.rs` imported `vstd::prelude::*` twice — `use vstd::prelude::*;`
(top, required so Verus attribute macros parse/erase correctly) and a redundant
`use ::vstd::prelude::*;` lower down.

**Why**: In the normal (non-Verus) `cargo build`, the Verus constructs are erased,
so the glob import is otherwise unused. With two identical glob imports, rustc
flags the second as `unused import`, which is promoted to a hard error under the
crate's `-D warnings`. This broke dual compilation (`./z build -- all-kernel`).
The sibling `mm::phys::upool` has only the single top-of-file import and builds
cleanly.

**Verification Failure**: Not a Verus failure (Verus build passed). Surfaced by
`./z build -- all-kernel`: `error: unused import: ::vstd::prelude::*`.

**How Verus Helped**: The dual-compilation requirement (Verus build + normal
build) exposed a latent redundant import that a Verus-only or normal-only build
in isolation would not necessarily flag the same way.

**Severity**: cosmetic / build-hygiene (no runtime effect).

**Suggested Fix / Auto-Fixed**: Yes — removed the redundant
`use ::vstd::prelude::*;`, keeping the single top-of-file `use vstd::prelude::*;`
(matching `upool.rs`). Both Verus verification and normal build pass afterwards.

## Note (not a bug) — `KernelFrame::new` retains `external_body`

The automated *strip-external-body* step removed `#[verus_verify(external_body)]`
from `KernelFrame::new`, leaving the source non-building (`error!` macro →
"Unsupported constant type") and, more fundamentally, unverifiable: `new`'s body
calls `crate::mm::virt::identity_map_page`, whose precondition is the **global**
`identity_map_view().inv()`. That fact belongs to the `mm::virt` identity-map
ghost token (a parameter-free singleton-global like `phys_view()`), which is not
realized in `mm::phys` and cannot be derived from the sole available precondition
`base.inv()`. No lemma/axiom yields `identity_map_view().inv()` unconditionally
(the view is `uninterp`). The attribute was therefore restored; `new` is listed
in `verus-ai-logs/tcb-allowed.md`. Same cross-module global-token deferral as
`frame::book`/`frame::alloc`. The in-scope siblings `base` and `drop` verify
in-body (no `admit`/`assume`/`external_body`).

1. // Copyright(c) The Maintainers of Nanvix.
2. // Licensed under the MIT License.
3. 
4. //! Kernel frame type.
5. //!
6. //! A [`KernelFrame`] represents a single page-sized physical frame allocated for kernel use.
7. //! It provides `Deref`/`DerefMut` for direct kernel access (identity-mapped) and frees the
8. //! underlying frame on drop via the global frame allocator.
9. 
10. //==================================================================================================
11. // Imports
12. //==================================================================================================
13. 
14. use vstd::prelude::*;
15. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
16. include!("kframe.spec.rs");
17. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
18. include!("kframe.proof.rs");
19. 
20. use crate::hal::mem::{
21.     Address,
22.     FrameAddress,
23.     PageAligned,
24.     PhysicalAddress,
25. };
26. use ::arch::mem;
27. use ::core::ops::{
28.     Deref,
29.     DerefMut,
30. };
31. use ::sys::error::Error;
32. 
33. //==================================================================================================
34. // Kernel Frame
35. //==================================================================================================
36. 
37. /// A type that represents a kernel frame.
38. #[derive(Debug)]
39. #[verus_verify(external_derive)]
40. pub struct KernelFrame {
41.     /// Frame address.
42.     base: FrameAddress,
43. }
44. 
45. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
46. verus! {
47. 
48. /// Abstract view of a kernel frame: the physical address of the owned frame.
49. impl View for KernelFrame {
50.     type V = int;
51. 
52.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int {
53.         self.base@
54.     }
55. }
56. 
57. } // verus!
58. 
59. // Dependency contract for the manager layer: wrapping a `FrameAddress` produces a handle whose
60. // abstract address is the same physical frame.
61. #[verus_verify]
62. impl KernelFrame {
63.     ///
64.     /// # Description
65.     ///
66.     /// Instantiates a kernel frame.
67.     ///
68.     /// # Parameters
69.     ///
70.     /// - `base`: Frame address.
71.     ///
72.     /// # Returns
73.     ///
74.     /// Upon success, a kernel frame is returned. Upon failure, an error is returned instead.
75.     ///
76.     // Dependency contract: wrapping a frame goes through `mm::virt::identity_map_page`, which
77.     // is outside the verification scope of `mm::phys`. On success the returned handle owns the
78.     // same physical frame that was passed in. `external_body` per `verus-ai-logs/tcb-allowed.md`:
79.     // the identity-mapping side effect lives in `mm::virt` and the body's `?`/log closures call
80.     // into that layer, so the wrap contract is trusted until `mm::virt` is verified.
81.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
82.     #[verus_spec(result =>
83.         requires
84.             base.inv(),
85.         ensures
86.             match result {
87.                 Ok(kf) => {
88.                     &&& kf@ == base@
89.                     &&& kf.inv()
90.                 },
91.                 Err(_) => true,
92.             },
93.     )]
94.     pub(super) fn new(base: FrameAddress) -> Result<Self, Error> {
95.         // Ensure the frame is identity-mapped in the kernel address space so that
96.         // Deref/DerefMut can safely access it. This lazily installs a page
97.         // table entry if needed (page tables come from a BSS pool, so no recursive frame
98.         // allocation occurs).
99.         let phys_addr: PageAligned<PhysicalAddress> =
100.             PageAligned::from_raw_value(base.into_raw_value()).map_err(|e| {
101.                 error!("frame base is not page-aligned: {e:?}");
102.                 e
103.             })?;
104.         crate::mm::virt::identity_map_page(phys_addr).map_err(|e| {
105.             error!("failed to identity-map frame: {:?}", e);
106.             e
107.         })?;
108. 
109.         Ok(Self { base })
110.     }
111. }
112. 
113. #[verus_verify]
114. impl KernelFrame {
115. 
116.     ///
117.     /// # Description
118.     ///
119.     /// Returns the base address of the target kernel frame.
120.     ///
121.     /// # Returns
122.     ///
123.     /// The base address of the target kernel frame.
124.     ///
125.     // Pure accessor: returns the owned frame's physical address unchanged. `result@ == self@`
126.     // gives `kpage` the exact address; `result.inv()` (page alignment carried from `self.inv()`)
127.     // lets `into_page_address` and the `KernelStack` arithmetic behind it proceed.
128.     #[verus_spec(result =>
129.         requires
130.             self.inv(),
131.         ensures
132.             result@ == self@,
133.             result.inv(),
134.     )]
135.     pub fn base(&self) -> FrameAddress {
136.         self.base
137.     }
138. }
139. 
140. impl KernelFrame {
141. 
142.     ///
143.     /// # Description
144.     ///
145.     /// Clears the target kernel frame.
146.     ///
147.     /// Uses the identity-map `memset` backend so that the write runs in the kernel address space.
148.     /// This avoids a page fault when the current CR3 points to a user page directory that lacks
149.     /// the PDE for this frame's physical address.
150.     ///
151.     pub fn clear(&mut self) -> Result<(), Error> {
152.         let base: *mut u8 = self.base.into_raw_value() as *mut u8;
153.         crate::mm::virt::memset(base, 0, mem::PAGE_SIZE).map_err(|e| {
154.             error!("memset failed: {:?}", e);
155.             e
156.         })
157.     }
158. }
159. 
160. /// # Safety
161. ///
162. /// `Deref` accesses the identity-mapped frame directly. The caller must ensure that the current
163. /// CR3 points to a page directory that has the relevant PDE for this frame's physical address
164. /// (i.e., the kernel page directory, or a user page directory into which the PDE has been
165. /// propagated via [`sync_kernel_pdes`](crate::mm::virt::sync_kernel_pdes)). For CR3-agnostic
166. /// writes, prefer [`KernelFrame::clear()`] which uses the identity-map `memset` backend.
167. impl Deref for KernelFrame {
168.     type Target = [u8];
169. 
170.     fn deref(&self) -> &Self::Target {
171.         let ptr: usize = self.base.into_raw_value();
172.         unsafe { core::slice::from_raw_parts(ptr as *const u8, mem::PAGE_SIZE) }
173.     }
174. }
175. 
176. /// # Safety
177. ///
178. /// See [`Deref`] impl — the same CR3 invariant applies.
179. impl DerefMut for KernelFrame {
180.     fn deref_mut(&mut self) -> &mut Self::Target {
181.         let ptr: usize = self.base.into_raw_value();
182.         unsafe { core::slice::from_raw_parts_mut(ptr as *mut u8, mem::PAGE_SIZE) }
183.     }
184. }
185. 
186. #[verus_verify]
187. impl Drop for KernelFrame {
188.     // Releasing the handle returns its physical frame to the global frame allocator via
189.     // `super::frame::free`, which is best-effort (`ensures true`) and `opens_invariants none`/
190.     // `no_unwind`, so `drop` makes no abstract postcondition. Callers (the manager error path,
191.     // `KernelStack::drop`) rely on this being the sole, complete deallocation step. Mirror of
192.     // `UserFrame::drop`.
193.     #[verus_spec(
194.         opens_invariants none
195.         no_unwind
196.     )]
197.     fn drop(&mut self) {
198.         if let Err(e) = super::frame::free(self.base) {
199.             #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
200.             error!("failed to free kernel frame: {:?}", e);
201.         }
202.     }
203. }
204.

3. impl KernelFrame {
4.     /// Well-formedness of a kernel-frame handle: its owned physical address is page aligned.
5.     ///
6.     /// Purely structural — it makes **no** ownership claim (it does not assert that the frame
7.     /// is allocated). Page alignment is the one caller-visible fact `base()`'s consumers rely on:
8.     /// `into_page_address` and the `KernelStack` index arithmetic behind it assume the returned
9.     /// `FrameAddress` is page aligned. Stated entirely on the abstract address `self@`, so it
10.     /// leaks no implementation detail. Mirror of `UserFrame::inv`.
11.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
12.         self@ % crate::hal::mem::spec_page_size() == 0
13.     }
14. }
15. 
16. } // verus!

29.   });
30.   ```
31.   The address handed to `new` always comes from a *successful* `frame::alloc()`.

33.   freed it / taken ownership of the physical frame on the error path).

40.   match FrameAddress::from_raw_value(raw_addr).and_then(KernelFrame::new) {
41.       Ok(kf) => frames.push(kf),

43.   }
44.   ```
45.   Addresses come from a contiguous allocation `frame::alloc_contiguous(count)`.
46.   Each `raw_addr` is page-aligned by construction. The spec requires that the
47.   pushed handle's view equals the contiguous physical address
48.   (`kernel_frames_contiguous`, `kernel_addr_set(final(frames)@)`), again relying

56.   drops already-wrapped `KernelFrame`s, "frees them via `KernelFrame::Drop`"
57.   (comment at `manager.rs:467`).

59.   each of which owns a `KernelFrame`, transitively dropping it.

69.   `self.kframe.base().into_page_address().into_virtual_address()`.

96.   passed in — `kf@ == base@`. The input `base` is always a valid, page-aligned

101.   No state guarantee beyond "the wrap failed".
102. - Callers don't care about: the identity-mapping side effect
103.   (`mm::virt::identity_map_page`), how page tables are installed, or any internal
104.   representation beyond the abstract address.
105.

107. - Callers assume: dropping frees the underlying physical frame exactly once via
108.   the global allocator, with no further action required from them.
109. - Callers don't care about: error handling inside drop (a failed free is only

114.   frame's `FrameAddress`, equal to the construction address (`result@ == self@`),
115.   and page-aligned so downstream page/virtual-address conversions are valid.
116. - Callers don't care about: how `base` is stored internally (field vs. computed).
117.

120. ## Abstract Resource
121. `KernelFrame` is an **owning handle to a single page-sized physical frame** that
122. is identity-mapped for kernel access. The module manages the ownership lifecycle
123. of one physical frame: `new` wraps a freshly allocated frame address into an
124. owning handle, `base` exposes that frame's physical address, and `drop` returns
125. the frame to the global frame allocator. Its `View` is the physical address
126. (`int`) of the owned frame.
127. 
128. ## Key Invariants (caller perspective)
129. - A `KernelFrame`'s abstract view is its physical frame address and never
130.   changes for the lifetime of the handle: `self@ == base@` from construction,
131.   and `base()` reports the same value.
132. - `new` preserves the input address on success (`kf@ == base@`) and does not
133.   consume the frame on failure.
134. - Each physical frame is owned by at most one live `KernelFrame`; dropping the
135.   handle frees that frame exactly once. Callers never double-free a wrapped frame.
136. - `base()` is pure: it does not mutate the handle or the allocator and returns a
137.   page-aligned `FrameAddress`.
138.

152. - Functions WITHOUT specs (in scope):
153.   - `KernelFrame::base` — no `#[verus_spec]`; needs `ensures result@ == self@`
154.     (pure accessor) for the `kpage` callers.
155.   - `KernelFrame::drop` — no `#[verus_spec]`; the manager error-path and
156.     `KernelStack::drop` rely on it freeing the frame, but its effect on the
157.     global allocator is not yet captured by a spec.
158.

161.   `lemma_kernel_alloc_one`). `base` and `drop` are unspecified.
162. - Strength: **adequate for `new`'s success path** (`kf@ == base@`), but the
163.   `Err(_) => true` ensures is weak; callers actually rely on the implicit
164.   contract that `new` does not free/consume the frame on failure (currently
165.   guaranteed only by `external_body` + manual free at the call site).
166. - View design: **caller-abstract** — `type V = int` (physical address) matches
167.   exactly what every caller uses (`kf@`, address comparisons, `kernel_addr_set`,
168.   `into_page_address`). It does not leak internal representation, so it is a good,
169.   stable abstraction.
170. 
171. ### Recommendations for View/spec design
172. - Keep `View::V = int` (the physical frame address) — all callers agree on this.
173. - Add a spec to `base`: `ensures result@ == self@` (pure accessor) so `kpage`
174.   conversions verify.
175. - Consider a spec for `drop` capturing the "frees the frame once" effect, so the
176.   manager error-path and stack teardown can reason about allocator state.

9. is stored, the page-table mechanics, the byte contents reachable through

23. }

26. This View was added when the manager layer (`alloc_kernel_frame`,
27. `alloc_many_kernel_frames`) was verified top-down. It is treated here as an
28. **input to evaluate**, not a finished design.

 # View Design: `mm::phys::kframe` (`KernelFrame`)
 
 ## Abstract Resource
 
 `KernelFrame` is an **owning handle to exactly one page-sized physical frame**.
 To the outside world it is a single value: *which physical frame this handle
 owns*. The only caller-observable abstract state is that frame's **physical
 address**. Everything else — the identity-mapping side effect, how the address
 is stored, the page-table mechanics, the byte contents reachable through
 `Deref` — is internal or out of scope.
 
 In-scope functions: `KernelFrame::new` (constructor), `KernelFrame::base`
 (query), `KernelFrame::drop` (destructor).
 
 ---
 
 ## Inherited View (from upstream `mm::phys` manager verification)
 
 ```rust
 impl View for KernelFrame {
     type V = int;
     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int { self.base@ }   // physical frame address
 }
 ```
 
 This View was added when the manager layer (`alloc_kernel_frame`,
 `alloc_many_kernel_frames`) was verified top-down. It is treated here as an
 **input to evaluate**, not a finished design.
 
 ### Evaluation against *all* callers
 
 | Caller | Uses `self@` as… | Verdict |
 |---|---|---|
 | `manager::alloc_kernel_frame` | the allocated address: `kf@ == frame_addr@`, `lemma_kernel_alloc_one(..., result->Ok_0@)` | ✅ address |
 | `manager::alloc_many_kernel_frames` | `kernel_frames_contiguous`, `kernel_addr_set(frames@)` — set/sequence of owned addresses | ✅ address |
 | `virt::kpage::KernelPage::base` | `kframe.base().into_page_address().into_virtual_address()` — needs the address + page-alignment | ✅ address |
 | `virt::kpage::KernelPage::frame_address` | returns `kframe.base()` verbatim | ✅ address |
 | `Drop` sites (manager error path, `KernelStack::drop`) | identity of the frame being freed exactly once | ✅ address |
 
 Every caller agrees: the abstract state is the **physical frame address**, an
 `int`. No caller needs anything else.
 
 **Decision: KEEP `type V = int` unchanged.** It already passes the
 substitution test from every caller's perspective (see Rationale). Nothing is
 renamed, added, or removed. The View definition is left exactly as inherited.
 
 ---

 The View is a primitive, not a struct:

 impl View for KernelFrame {
     type V = int;                       // the physical address of the owned frame

 }

# Kernel Development

Use this skill when the user asks about developing, modifying, or debugging the Nanvix microkernel.
The kernel is a `#![no_std]` Rust binary targeting x86 (32-bit) and lives in `src/kernel/`.

## Architecture Overview

The kernel is a freestanding binary (`#![no_std]`,
`#![no_main]`) that runs in ring 0 on x86. Entry point is
`src/kernel/src/kmain.rs`.

### Key Modules

| Module   | Path                      | Purpose               |
|----------|---------------------------|-----------------------|
| `hal`    | `src/kernel/src/hal/`     | Hardware Abstraction. |
| `mm`     | `src/kernel/src/mm/`      | Memory Management.    |
| `pm`     | `src/kernel/src/pm/`      | Process Management.   |
| `ipc`    | `src/kernel/src/ipc/`     | IPC (mailboxes).      |
| `event`  | `src/kernel/src/event/`   | Event subsystem.      |
| `io`     | `src/kernel/src/io/`      | I/O subsystem.        |
| `kcall`  | `src/kernel/src/kcall/`   | Kernel call dispatch. |
| `kargs`  | `src/kernel/src/kargs.rs` | Boot args parsing.    |
| `kimage` | `src/kernel/src/kimage.rs`| Kernel image mgmt.    |
| `klog`   | `src/kernel/src/klog.rs`  | Kernel logging.       |
| `kpanic` | `src/kernel/src/kpanic.rs`| Panic handler.        |
| `uart`   | `src/kernel/src/uart.rs`  | UART serial driver.   |

### Machine Configurations

The kernel supports multiple machine types via Cargo
feature flags:

- `microvm` (default) — Lightweight VM for KVM.

### Virtual Memory Layout

- `KERNEL_BASE_RAW` to `KPOOL_BASE_RAW` — Kernel binary.
- `KPOOL_BASE_RAW` to `USER_BASE_RAW` — Kernel pool.
- `USER_BASE_RAW` to `USER_MMAP_BASE_RAW` — User binary.
- `USER_MMAP_BASE_RAW` to `USER_LIBS_BASE_RAW` — Mapped.
- `USER_LIBS_BASE_RAW` to `USER_HEAP_BASE_RAW` — Libs.
- `USER_HEAP_BASE_RAW` to `USER_HEAP_END_RAW` — Heap.
- `USER_STACK_TOP_RAW` to `USER_STACK_BASE_RAW` — Stack.

## Building the Kernel

```bash
./z build -- kernel
```

The kernel uses a custom Cargo target
(`build/targets/x86-kernel.json`) and custom linker scripts
(`build/kernel/`). Kernel builds disable sccache to avoid
issues with `compiler_builtins`.

## Key Dependencies

The kernel depends on workspace libraries:

- `arch` — Architecture abstractions.
- `bitmap` — Bitmap data structure.
- `config` — Compile-time configuration.
- `type-safe` — Type-safe wrappers.
- `raw-array` — Fixed-size arrays.
- `slab` — Slab allocator.
- `sys` — System-level types (kcall, IPC, MM, PM).

## Coding Rules (Kernel-Specific)

- All kernel code is `#![no_std]` — only `core` and `alloc`
  are available.
- No `panic!`, `unwrap()`, or `expect()` in production
  kernel code.
- Use explicit type annotations everywhere.
- Prefix imports with `::`.
- Minimize `unsafe` blocks and document safety invariants.
- Log errors with `error!` macro before returning `Err`.
- Use kernel-specific Cargo commands:
  `KERNEL_CARGO_BUILD_CMD`.
- Kernel configuration is in `build/kernel_config.toml`.

## Kernel Calls (System Calls)

Kernel calls are dispatched through
`src/kernel/src/kcall/dispatcher.rs`. Each subsystem (PM,
MM, IPC, Event, IO) registers its own kernel call handlers
in its respective `kcall/` subdirectory.

22.

24.   ```rust
25.   let frame_addr: FrameAddress = frame::alloc()?;
26.   let result = KernelFrame::new(frame_addr).inspect_err(|e| {
27.       // on failure, free the raw frame again
28.       if let Err(free_err) = frame::free(frame_addr) { ... }
29.   });
30.   ```
31.   The address handed to `new` always comes from a *successful* `frame::alloc()`.
32.   On `new` failure the caller frees `frame_addr` itself (so `new` must NOT have
33.   freed it / taken ownership of the physical frame on the error path).
34.   On success the manager proof relies on `result->Ok_0@` being the allocated
35.   address (`lemma_kernel_alloc_one(g_old, self@, result->Ok_0@)`), i.e. it needs
36.   `kf@ == frame_addr@`.
37. 
38. - `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs:464` — `alloc_many_kernel_frames`:
39.   ```rust
40.   match FrameAddress::from_raw_value(raw_addr).and_then(KernelFrame::new) {
41.       Ok(kf) => frames.push(kf),
42.       Err(e) => { frames.clear(); /* free remaining raw frames */ }
43.   }
44.   ```
45.   Addresses come from a contiguous allocation `frame::alloc_contiguous(count)`.
46.   Each `raw_addr` is page-aligned by construction. The spec requires that the
47.   pushed handle's view equals the contiguous physical address
48.   (`kernel_frames_contiguous`, `kernel_addr_set(final(frames)@)`), again relying
49.   on `kf@ == base@`.
50. 
51. ### `KernelFrame::drop` — trait `Drop`, implicit (compiler-dispatched)
52. No explicit call sites; runs when a `KernelFrame` goes out of scope. Implicit
53. drop sites observed:
54. 
55. - `mm::phys::manager::alloc_many_kernel_frames` error path: `frames.clear()`
56.   drops already-wrapped `KernelFrame`s, "frees them via `KernelFrame::Drop`"
57.   (comment at `manager.rs:467`).
58. - `mm::kstack::KernelStack::drop` (`kstack.rs:334`) pops and drops `KernelPage`s,
59.   each of which owns a `KernelFrame`, transitively dropping it.
60. - Any `KernelFrame`/`KernelPage`/`KernelStack` value that goes out of scope.
61. 
62. The drop body calls `super::frame::free(self.base)` — i.e. dropping a handle
63. returns its physical frame to the global allocator.
64. 
65. ### `KernelFrame::base` — `pub`, 2 call sites
66. Both in `mm::virt::kpage`:
67. 
68. - `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/kpage.rs:58` — `KernelPage::base`:
69.   `self.kframe.base().into_page_address().into_virtual_address()`.
70. - `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/kpage.rs:74` — `KernelPage::frame_address`:
71.   returns `self.kframe.base()` directly.
72. 
73. Both callers treat `base()` as a pure accessor that yields the frame's
74. `FrameAddress`, then convert it to page/virtual addresses. They rely on the
75. returned value being exactly the address the frame was created with (and being
76. page-aligned, since `into_page_address` and `KernelStack` arithmetic assume it).
77. 
78. ---
79. 
80. ## Trait Obligations
81. - Trait `Drop` (`KernelFrame::drop`) — expected semantics: releasing the handle
82.   returns ownership of the underlying physical frame to the global frame
83.   allocator exactly once (`super::frame::free(self.base)`). Callers
84.   (`alloc_many_kernel_frames` error path, `KernelStack::drop`) depend on drop
85.   being the *sole* and *complete* deallocation step — they do not free the frame
86.   themselves once it has been wrapped in a `KernelFrame`.
87. - Traits `Deref` / `DerefMut` — out of scope here; provide identity-mapped slice
88.   access (CR3 invariant documented in source).
89. 
90. ---

94. ### `KernelFrame::new`
95. - Callers assume: on `Ok(kf)`, the handle owns the *same* physical frame that was
96.   passed in — `kf@ == base@`. The input `base` is always a valid, page-aligned
97.   address obtained from a successful `frame::alloc()` / `alloc_contiguous()`
98.   (i.e. `base.inv()` holds).
99. - Callers assume: on `Err(_)`, `new` did **not** take ownership / did not free the
100.   frame — the caller is responsible for freeing `base` (it does so explicitly).
101.   No state guarantee beyond "the wrap failed".
102. - Callers don't care about: the identity-mapping side effect
103.   (`mm::virt::identity_map_page`), how page tables are installed, or any internal
104.   representation beyond the abstract address.
105. 
106. ### `KernelFrame::drop`
107. - Callers assume: dropping frees the underlying physical frame exactly once via
108.   the global allocator, with no further action required from them.

1. # View Design: `mm::phys::kframe` (`KernelFrame`)
2. 
3. ## Abstract Resource
4. 
5. `KernelFrame` is an **owning handle to exactly one page-sized physical frame**.
6. To the outside world it is a single value: *which physical frame this handle
7. owns*. The only caller-observable abstract state is that frame's **physical
8. address**. Everything else — the identity-mapping side effect, how the address
9. is stored, the page-table mechanics, the byte contents reachable through
10. `Deref` — is internal or out of scope.
11. 
12. In-scope functions: `KernelFrame::new` (constructor), `KernelFrame::base`
13. (query), `KernelFrame::drop` (destructor).
14. 
15. ---
16. 
17. ## Inherited View (from upstream `mm::phys` manager verification)
18. 
19. ```rust
20. impl View for KernelFrame {
21.     type V = int;
22.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int { self.base@ }   // physical frame address
23. }
24. ```
25. 
26. This View was added when the manager layer (`alloc_kernel_frame`,
27. `alloc_many_kernel_frames`) was verified top-down. It is treated here as an
28. **input to evaluate**, not a finished design.
29. 
30. ### Evaluation against *all* callers
31. 
32. | Caller | Uses `self@` as… | Verdict |
33. |---|---|---|
34. | `manager::alloc_kernel_frame` | the allocated address: `kf@ == frame_addr@`, `lemma_kernel_alloc_one(..., result->Ok_0@)` | ✅ address |
35. | `manager::alloc_many_kernel_frames` | `kernel_frames_contiguous`, `kernel_addr_set(frames@)` — set/sequence of owned addresses | ✅ address |
36. | `virt::kpage::KernelPage::base` | `kframe.base().into_page_address().into_virtual_address()` — needs the address + page-alignment | ✅ address |
37. | `virt::kpage::KernelPage::frame_address` | returns `kframe.base()` verbatim | ✅ address |
38. | `Drop` sites (manager error path, `KernelStack::drop`) | identity of the frame being freed exactly once | ✅ address |
39. 
40. Every caller agrees: the abstract state is the **physical frame address**, an
41. `int`. No caller needs anything else.
42. 
43. **Decision: KEEP `type V = int` unchanged.** It already passes the
44. substitution test from every caller's perspective (see Rationale). Nothing is
45. renamed, added, or removed. The View definition is left exactly as inherited.
46. 
47. ---
48. 
49. ## View Struct
50. 
51. The View is a primitive, not a struct:
52. 
53. ```rust
54. impl View for KernelFrame {
55.     type V = int;                       // the physical address of the owned frame
56.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int { /* maps impl field -> address */ }
57. }
58. ```
59. 
60. - `view()` stays **`closed`**: public so callers write `kf@`, closed so the
61.   field-level mapping (currently `self.base@`) does not leak.
62. - The value space is `int` — the mathematical physical address. (Per the
63.   view-design exception, an address could keep `usize`; here the upstream View
64.   and the whole `FrameAddress`/`Inner` address algebra already work in `int`
65.   via `View::V = int`, so `int` is the consistent, cast-free choice.)
66. 
67. A wrapper struct (`KernelFrameView { addr: int }`) was considered and
68. **rejected** — see Rejected Alternatives.
69. 
70. ---
71. 
72. ## Well-formedness Invariant
73. 
74. `KernelFrame` currently has **no** `inv()`. Callers of `base()`
75. (`into_page_address`, and the page/stack address arithmetic behind it) rely on
76. the owned address being **page-aligned**. This is a caller-visible constraint
77. on the abstract state, so it belongs in `inv()`.
78. 
79. **Final decision (spec phase): single `inv()`, mirroring the verified sibling
80. `UserFrame::inv`.** The originally-sketched `internal_inv()` placeholder
81. (`pub closed spec fn internal_inv(&self) -> bool { true }`) was dropped: it would
82. be permanently `true` (the closed view `self@ == self.base@` already exposes the
83. alignment fact directly, so no implementation-consistency clause is needed), and
84. the `spec-design` skill discourages extra `pub spec fn`s on `impl MyType` beyond
85. `view`/`inv`. The result is identical in shape to `UserFrame`:
86. 
87. ```rust
88. impl KernelFrame {
89.     // Caller-visible well-formedness: the owned frame address is page-aligned.
90.     // Stated purely on the int view via the shared spec_page_size(); leaks no
91.     // implementation detail. Mirror of UserFrame::inv.
92.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
93.         self@ % spec_page_size() == 0
94.     }
95. }
96. ```
97. 
98. - `inv()` is **`pub open`** so callers can establish and consume it.
99. - `spec_page_size()` is the same `pub uninterp spec fn` already used by
100.   `FrameAddress::inv` (`self@ % spec_page_size() == 0`); reusing it keeps the
101.   alignment notion identical across the two types.
102. - No `internal_inv()` is defined; the alignment fact follows on the `new` /
103.   `base` paths directly from the required `base.inv()` / `self.inv()`.
104. 
105. No other `pub spec fn` is added to `impl KernelFrame` beyond `view` and `inv`.
106. 
107. ---
108. 
109. ## Spec Transition Functions
110. 
111. **There are none — and that is a deliberate, substitution-tested result.**
112. 
113. A `KernelFrame`'s abstract view is fixed at construction and **never changes**
114. for the lifetime of the handle. The in-scope API confirms this:
115. 
116. - `new(base)` is a **constructor**: it produces a fresh handle whose view *is*
117.   the input address. The contract is a constructor postcondition, not a
118.   transition on an existing view:
119. 
120.   ```rust
121.   // new (already external_body per tcb-allowed.md; keep its existing spec,
122.   // optionally surface the invariant it already guarantees):
123.   ensures match result {
124.       Ok(kf) => kf@ == base@ && kf.inv(),   // inv follows from required base.inv()
125.       Err(_) => true,                       // no ownership taken on failure
126.   }
127.   ```
128. 
129. - `base(&self)` is a **pure query** — no view change. Needed new spec:
130. 
131.   ```rust
132.   fn base(&self) -> (result: FrameAddress)
133.       requires self.inv(),
134.       ensures  result@ == self@ && result.inv();
135.   ```
136. 
137.   `result@ == self@` gives `kpage` the exact address; `result.inv()` (carried
138.   from `self.inv()`'s alignment clause) lets `into_page_address` and the stack
139.   arithmetic proceed.
140. 
141. - `drop(&mut self)` is a **destructor**. Its effect is *not* a transition on
142.   `KernelFrame`'s own view (the value is consumed). Dropping returns the frame
143.   `old(self)@` to the **global frame allocator**, so its postcondition is
144.   written against the allocator's View (`FrameAllocView` / `phys_view().frames`,
145.   the same View the manager already reasons over), e.g. "after drop,
146.   `old(self)@` is no longer allocated / is back in the free partition, and no
147.   other frame's status changes." Because that state lives in the allocator's
148.   abstraction, **no field is needed on `KernelFrameView` to express it**.
149. 
150. Consequently `impl KernelFrame`'s View needs no `spec_*` mutator helpers: the
151. view is immutable per handle, the only state change in the module
152. (allocation/free) is owned by the allocator's View.
153. 
154. ---
155. 
156. ## Design Rationale
157. 
158. ### Field: the view value `self@ : int` — the physical frame address
159. - **Why needed.** It is the one thing every caller reasons about: the manager
160.   proves the wrapped address equals the allocated address and builds
161.   `kernel_addr_set` / contiguity facts from it; `kpage` converts it to page and
162.   virtual addresses; `drop` frees *that* address. There is no caller use of
163.   `KernelFrame` that does not reduce to its address.
164. - **Substitution test.** *If `KernelFrame` were rewritten to store a raw
165.   `usize`, a frame number, or to compute the address on the fly instead of
166.   holding a `FrameAddress` — would "the physical frame address" still make
167.   sense?* **Yes.** Any owning-frame-handle implementation must denote *some*
168.   physical frame; its address is the implementation-independent identity of
169.   what is owned. ✅
170. - **Caller-only.** A caller understands "the physical address of the frame this
171.   handle owns" with zero knowledge of the internal field, the identity map, or
172.   page tables.
173. 
174. ### `inv()` clause: `self@ % spec_page_size() == 0` (page-aligned)
175. - **Why needed.** `base()` returns a `FrameAddress` that downstream code feeds
176.   to `into_page_address` and to `KernelStack` index arithmetic, both of which
177.   assume page alignment. Collecting this into `inv()` (instead of re-deriving it
178.   at every call site) follows the "missing wf()" anti-pattern fix.
179. - **Substitution test.** Alignment is a property of *what a physical frame is*
180.   (page-sized, page-aligned), not of how the handle stores it. Any
181.   implementation that owns a real frame yields a page-aligned address. ✅
182. - **Caller-abstract.** Stated purely on `self@` using the shared
183.   `spec_page_size()`; no implementation detail appears.
184. 
185. ### `internal_inv()` left as `true`
186. - Per methodology, implementation-consistency facts (here: "the stored
187.   `FrameAddress` satisfies its own `inv`") require seeing impl fields, so they
188.   are deferred to the spec phase. The caller-visible consequence (alignment) is
189.   already exposed through `inv()`.
190. 
191. ### Why no spec transition functions
192. - The handle's view is immutable; the only mutation in the module's lifecycle
193.   (a frame leaving the free partition on `new`'s upstream `alloc`, and returning
194.   on `drop`) is state of the **allocator**, captured by `FrameAllocView`, not by
195.   this per-object View. Modeling it here would duplicate (and risk
196.   desynchronizing) the allocator's abstraction.
197. 
198. ---
199. 
200. ## Rejected Alternatives
201. 
202. 1. **Wrapper struct `KernelFrameView { addr: int }`.**
203.    Rejected for minimality. A one-field struct adds a layer of `.addr`
204.    projections to every caller spec (`kf@.addr` vs `kf@`) and a `view()` that
205.    constructs the struct, with zero added information. `type V = int` is the
206.    simpler, already-adopted, caller-agreed abstraction. The `inv()` predicate
207.    lives perfectly well on `impl KernelFrame`.
208. 
209. 2. **Add an `allocated: bool` / ownership flag, or an allocator reference, to
210.    the View.**
211.    Rejected as an abstraction leak / wrong owner. Whether a frame is allocated
212.    is global allocator state, already modeled by `FrameAllocView`
213.    (`phys_view().frames`). The manager error path and `KernelStack::drop` reason
214.    about "freed exactly once" through the allocator's view, not through a flag
215.    on the handle. Duplicating it here would create two sources of truth that
216.    must be kept in sync. `drop`'s contract is therefore written against the
217.    allocator's View, leaving `KernelFrame`'s View minimal.
218. 
219. 3. **Add a `mapped: bool` (identity-mapping) field.**
220.    Rejected. The caller analysis is explicit: callers *do not care* about the
221.    identity-mapping side effect of `new`. It is an internal effect of
222.    `mm::virt::identity_map_page` (outside `mm::phys` scope) and observable to no
223.    in-scope caller. Including it would leak HOW the handle is set up.
224. 
225. 4. **Add the frame's byte contents (e.g. `Seq<u8>` / a `PointsTo`) to the
226.    View.**
227.    Rejected for this scope. Byte contents are only relevant to `Deref`,
228.    `DerefMut`, and `clear` — all explicitly **out of scope** and not to be
229.    touched. The in-scope functions (`new`, `base`, `drop`) concern only frame
230.    *ownership/identity*, i.e. the address. If/when the access functions are
231.    verified, the natural model for their bytes is a `PointsTo` over the
232.    identity-mapped region (keyed by `self@`), not a field baked into this
233.    ownership View — so adding it now would be premature and would destabilize
234.    the View the current callers already depend on.
235. 
236. 5. **Change `view()` to `usize` instead of `int`.**
237.    Rejected for consistency. The entire surrounding address algebra
238.    (`FrameAddress`, `Inner`, `FrameAllocView`, the manager's
239.    `kernel_addr_set`/contiguity lemmas) is expressed with `View::V = int`.
240.    Switching this one View to `usize` would force casts at every interface with
241.    those specs for no benefit; the inherited `int` view is correct as-is.
242. 
243. 6. **Strengthen `new`'s `Err(_) => true` into an explicit "frame not consumed"
244.    postcondition.**
245.    Considered (the caller does rely on `new` not freeing `base` on failure), but
246.    **out of scope for View design** and partly outside this module: the
247.    no-consume guarantee on the error path is currently provided by `new` being a

 # View Design: `mm::phys::kframe` (`KernelFrame`)
 
 ## Abstract Resource
 
 `KernelFrame` is an **owning handle to exactly one page-sized physical frame**.
 To the outside world it is a single value: *which physical frame this handle
 owns*. The only caller-observable abstract state is that frame's **physical
 address**. Everything else — the identity-mapping side effect, how the address
 is stored, the page-table mechanics, the byte contents reachable through
 `Deref` — is internal or out of scope.
 
 In-scope functions: `KernelFrame::new` (constructor), `KernelFrame::base`
 (query), `KernelFrame::drop` (destructor).
 
 ---
 
 ## Inherited View (from upstream `mm::phys` manager verification)
 
 ```rust
 impl View for KernelFrame {
     type V = int;
     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int { self.base@ }   // physical frame address
 }
 ```
 
 This View was added when the manager layer (`alloc_kernel_frame`,
 `alloc_many_kernel_frames`) was verified top-down. It is treated here as an
 **input to evaluate**, not a finished design.
 
 ### Evaluation against *all* callers
 
 | Caller | Uses `self@` as… | Verdict |
 |---|---|---|
 | `manager::alloc_kernel_frame` | the allocated address: `kf@ == frame_addr@`, `lemma_kernel_alloc_one(..., result->Ok_0@)` | ✅ address |
 | `manager::alloc_many_kernel_frames` | `kernel_frames_contiguous`, `kernel_addr_set(frames@)` — set/sequence of owned addresses | ✅ address |
 | `virt::kpage::KernelPage::base` | `kframe.base().into_page_address().into_virtual_address()` — needs the address + page-alignment | ✅ address |
 | `virt::kpage::KernelPage::frame_address` | returns `kframe.base()` verbatim | ✅ address |
 | `Drop` sites (manager error path, `KernelStack::drop`) | identity of the frame being freed exactly once | ✅ address |
 
 Every caller agrees: the abstract state is the **physical frame address**, an
 `int`. No caller needs anything else.
 
 **Decision: KEEP `type V = int` unchanged.** It already passes the
 substitution test from every caller's perspective (see Rationale). Nothing is
 renamed, added, or removed. The View definition is left exactly as inherited.
 
 ---
 
 ## View Struct
 
 The View is a primitive, not a struct:
 
 ```rust
 impl View for KernelFrame {
     type V = int;                       // the physical address of the owned frame
     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int { /* maps impl field -> address */ }
 }
 ```
 
 - `view()` stays **`closed`**: public so callers write `kf@`, closed so the
   field-level mapping (currently `self.base@`) does not leak.
 - The value space is `int` — the mathematical physical address. (Per the
   view-design exception, an address could keep `usize`; here the upstream View
   and the whole `FrameAddress`/`Inner` address algebra already work in `int`
   via `View::V = int`, so `int` is the consistent, cast-free choice.)
 
 A wrapper struct (`KernelFrameView { addr: int }`) was considered and
 **rejected** — see Rejected Alternatives.
 
 ---
 
 ## Well-formedness Invariant
 
 `KernelFrame` currently has **no** `inv()`. Callers of `base()`
 (`into_page_address`, and the page/stack address arithmetic behind it) rely on
 the owned address being **page-aligned**. This is a caller-visible constraint
 on the abstract state, so it belongs in `inv()`.
 
 **Final decision (spec phase): single `inv()`, mirroring the verified sibling
 `UserFrame::inv`.** The originally-sketched `internal_inv()` placeholder
 (`pub closed spec fn internal_inv(&self) -> bool { true }`) was dropped: it would
 be permanently `true` (the closed view `self@ == self.base@` already exposes the
 alignment fact directly, so no implementation-consistency clause is needed), and
 the `spec-design` skill discourages extra `pub spec fn`s on `impl MyType` beyond
 `view`/`inv`. The result is identical in shape to `UserFrame`:
 
 ```rust
 impl KernelFrame {
     // Caller-visible well-formedness: the owned frame address is page-aligned.
     // Stated purely on the int view via the shared spec_page_size(); leaks no
     // implementation detail. Mirror of UserFrame::inv.
     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
         self@ % spec_page_size() == 0
     }
 }
 ```
 
 - `inv()` is **`pub open`** so callers can establish and consume it.
 - `spec_page_size()` is the same `pub uninterp spec fn` already used by
   `FrameAddress::inv` (`self@ % spec_page_size() == 0`); reusing it keeps the
   alignment notion identical across the two types.
 - No `internal_inv()` is defined; the alignment fact follows on the `new` /
   `base` paths directly from the required `base.inv()` / `self.inv()`.
 
 No other `pub spec fn` is added to `impl KernelFrame` beyond `view` and `inv`.
 
 ---
 
 ## Spec Transition Functions
 
 **There are none — and that is a deliberate, substitution-tested result.**
 
 A `KernelFrame`'s abstract view is fixed at construction and **never changes**
 for the lifetime of the handle. The in-scope API confirms this:
 
 - `new(base)` is a **constructor**: it produces a fresh handle whose view *is*
   the input address. The contract is a constructor postcondition, not a
   transition on an existing view:
 
   ```rust
   // new (already external_body per tcb-allowed.md; keep its existing spec,
   // optionally surface the invariant it already guarantees):
   ensures match result {
       Ok(kf) => kf@ == base@ && kf.inv(),   // inv follows from required base.inv()
       Err(_) => true,                       // no ownership taken on failure
   }
   ```
 
 - `base(&self)` is a **pure query** — no view change. Needed new spec:
 
   ```rust
   fn base(&self) -> (result: FrameAddress)
       requires self.inv(),
       ensures  result@ == self@ && result.inv();
   ```
 
   `result@ == self@` gives `kpage` the exact address; `result.inv()` (carried
   from `self.inv()`'s alignment clause) lets `into_page_address` and the stack
   arithmetic proceed.
 
 - `drop(&mut self)` is a **destructor**. Its effect is *not* a transition on
   `KernelFrame`'s own view (the value is consumed). Dropping returns the frame
   `old(self)@` to the **global frame allocator**, so its postcondition is
   written against the allocator's View (`FrameAllocView` / `phys_view().frames`,
   the same View the manager already reasons over), e.g. "after drop,
   `old(self)@` is no longer allocated / is back in the free partition, and no
   other frame's status changes." Because that state lives in the allocator's
   abstraction, **no field is needed on `KernelFrameView` to express it**.
 
 Consequently `impl KernelFrame`'s View needs no `spec_*` mutator helpers: the
 view is immutable per handle, the only state change in the module
 (allocation/free) is owned by the allocator's View.
 
 ---
 
 ## Design Rationale
 
 ### Field: the view value `self@ : int` — the physical frame address
 - **Why needed.** It is the one thing every caller reasons about: the manager
   proves the wrapped address equals the allocated address and builds
   `kernel_addr_set` / contiguity facts from it; `kpage` converts it to page and
   virtual addresses; `drop` frees *that* address. There is no caller use of
   `KernelFrame` that does not reduce to its address.
 - **Substitution test.** *If `KernelFrame` were rewritten to store a raw
   `usize`, a frame number, or to compute the address on the fly instead of
   holding a `FrameAddress` — would "the physical frame address" still make
   sense?* **Yes.** Any owning-frame-handle implementation must denote *some*
   physical frame; its address is the implementation-independent identity of
   what is owned. ✅
 - **Caller-only.** A caller understands "the physical address of the frame this
   handle owns" with zero knowledge of the internal field, the identity map, or
   page tables.
 
 ### `inv()` clause: `self@ % spec_page_size() == 0` (page-aligned)
 - **Why needed.** `base()` returns a `FrameAddress` that downstream code feeds
   to `into_page_address` and to `KernelStack` index arithmetic, both of which
   assume page alignment. Collecting this into `inv()` (instead of re-deriving it
   at every call site) follows the "missing wf()" anti-pattern fix.
 - **Substitution test.** Alignment is a property of *what a physical frame is*
   (page-sized, page-aligned), not of how the handle stores it. Any
   implementation that owns a real frame yields a page-aligned address. ✅
 - **Caller-abstract.** Stated purely on `self@` using the shared
   `spec_page_size()`; no implementation detail appears.
 
 ### `internal_inv()` left as `true`
 - Per methodology, implementation-consistency facts (here: "the stored
   `FrameAddress` satisfies its own `inv`") require seeing impl fields, so they
   are deferred to the spec phase. The caller-visible consequence (alignment) is
   already exposed through `inv()`.
 
 ### Why no spec transition functions
 - The handle's view is immutable; the only mutation in the module's lifecycle
   (a frame leaving the free partition on `new`'s upstream `alloc`, and returning
   on `drop`) is state of the **allocator**, captured by `FrameAllocView`, not by
   this per-object View. Modeling it here would duplicate (and risk
   desynchronizing) the allocator's abstraction.
 
 ---
 
 ## Rejected Alternatives
 
 1. **Wrapper struct `KernelFrameView { addr: int }`.**
    Rejected for minimality. A one-field struct adds a layer of `.addr`
    projections to every caller spec (`kf@.addr` vs `kf@`) and a `view()` that
    constructs the struct, with zero added information. `type V = int` is the
    simpler, already-adopted, caller-agreed abstraction. The `inv()` predicate
    lives perfectly well on `impl KernelFrame`.
 
 2. **Add an `allocated: bool` / ownership flag, or an allocator reference, to
    the View.**
    Rejected as an abstraction leak / wrong owner. Whether a frame is allocated
    is global allocator state, already modeled by `FrameAllocView`
    (`phys_view().frames`). The manager error path and `KernelStack::drop` reason
    about "freed exactly once" through the allocator's view, not through a flag
    on the handle. Duplicating it here would create two sources of truth that
    must be kept in sync. `drop`'s contract is therefore written against the
    allocator's View, leaving `KernelFrame`'s View minimal.
 
 3. **Add a `mapped: bool` (identity-mapping) field.**
    Rejected. The caller analysis is explicit: callers *do not care* about the
    identity-mapping side effect of `new`. It is an internal effect of
    `mm::virt::identity_map_page` (outside `mm::phys` scope) and observable to no
    in-scope caller. Including it would leak HOW the handle is set up.
 
 4. **Add the frame's byte contents (e.g. `Seq<u8>` / a `PointsTo`) to the
    View.**
    Rejected for this scope. Byte contents are only relevant to `Deref`,
    `DerefMut`, and `clear` — all explicitly **out of scope** and not to be
    touched. The in-scope functions (`new`, `base`, `drop`) concern only frame
    *ownership/identity*, i.e. the address. If/when the access functions are
    verified, the natural model for their bytes is a `PointsTo` over the
    identity-mapped region (keyed by `self@`), not a field baked into this
    ownership View — so adding it now would be premature and would destabilize
    the View the current callers already depend on.
 
 5. **Change `view()` to `usize` instead of `int`.**
    Rejected for consistency. The entire surrounding address algebra
    (`FrameAddress`, `Inner`, `FrameAllocView`, the manager's
    `kernel_addr_set`/contiguity lemmas) is expressed with `View::V = int`.
    Switching this one View to `usize` would force casts at every interface with
    those specs for no benefit; the inherited `int` view is correct as-is.
 
 6. **Strengthen `new`'s `Err(_) => true` into an explicit "frame not consumed"
    postcondition.**
    Considered (the caller does rely on `new` not freeing `base` on failure), but
    **out of scope for View design** and partly outside this module: the
    no-consume guarantee on the error path is currently provided by `new` being a
    trusted `external_body` dependency contract (it never touches the global
    allocator on `Err`) plus the caller's explicit `frame::free(base)` cleanup.
    The View needs no field to express it. Noted here for the spec phase; the
    View design is unaffected.
 
 ---
 
 ## Quality Review
 
 | Criterion | Check |
 |---|---|
 | **Substitution** | The address (and its page-alignment) survive any rewrite of how the handle stores/derives the frame. ✅ |
 | **Caller-only** | Every caller reads `kf@` as "the owned frame's physical address" with no impl knowledge. ✅ |
 | **Complete** | All in-scope caller-observable concepts — owned-frame identity (`new`/`base`/`drop`), set/contiguity facts, page-aligned conversions — are expressible from `self@` + `inv()`. Allocator/ownership effects of `drop` are covered by the existing allocator View. ✅ |
 | **Minimal** | Single `int` view; the one `inv()` clause is used by every `base()` caller. No unused fields. ✅ |
 | **No code-as-spec** | The View states *what* (a physical address, page-aligned), never *how* (identity map, page tables, field layout). ✅ |

1. # View Design: `mm::phys::kframe` (`KernelFrame`)
2. 
3. ## Abstract Resource
4. 
5. `KernelFrame` is an **owning handle to exactly one page-sized physical frame**.
6. To the outside world it is a single value: *which physical frame this handle
7. owns*. The only caller-observable abstract state is that frame's **physical
8. address**. Everything else — the identity-mapping side effect, how the address
9. is stored, the page-table mechanics, the byte contents reachable through
10. `Deref` — is internal or out of scope.
11. 
12. In-scope functions: `KernelFrame::new` (constructor), `KernelFrame::base`
13. (query), `KernelFrame::drop` (destructor).
14. 
15. ---
16. 
17. ## Inherited View (from upstream `mm::phys` manager verification)
18. 
19. ```rust
20. impl View for KernelFrame {
21.     type V = int;
22.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int { self.base@ }   // physical frame address
23. }
24. ```
25. 
26. This View was added when the manager layer (`alloc_kernel_frame`,
27. `alloc_many_kernel_frames`) was verified top-down. It is treated here as an
28. **input to evaluate**, not a finished design.
29. 
30. ### Evaluation against *all* callers
31. 
32. | Caller | Uses `self@` as… | Verdict |
33. |---|---|---|
34. | `manager::alloc_kernel_frame` | the allocated address: `kf@ == frame_addr@`, `lemma_kernel_alloc_one(..., result->Ok_0@)` | ✅ address |
35. | `manager::alloc_many_kernel_frames` | `kernel_frames_contiguous`, `kernel_addr_set(frames@)` — set/sequence of owned addresses | ✅ address |
36. | `virt::kpage::KernelPage::base` | `kframe.base().into_page_address().into_virtual_address()` — needs the address + page-alignment | ✅ address |
37. | `virt::kpage::KernelPage::frame_address` | returns `kframe.base()` verbatim | ✅ address |
38. | `Drop` sites (manager error path, `KernelStack::drop`) | identity of the frame being freed exactly once | ✅ address |
39. 
40. Every caller agrees: the abstract state is the **physical frame address**, an
41. `int`. No caller needs anything else.
42. 
43. **Decision: KEEP `type V = int` unchanged.** It already passes the
44. substitution test from every caller's perspective (see Rationale). Nothing is
45. renamed, added, or removed. The View definition is left exactly as inherited.
46. 
47. ---
48. 
49. ## View Struct
50. 
51. The View is a primitive, not a struct:
52. 
53. ```rust
54. impl View for KernelFrame {
55.     type V = int;                       // the physical address of the owned frame
56.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int { /* maps impl field -> address */ }
57. }
58. ```
59. 
60. - `view()` stays **`closed`**: public so callers write `kf@`, closed so the
61.   field-level mapping (currently `self.base@`) does not leak.
62. - The value space is `int` — the mathematical physical address. (Per the
63.   view-design exception, an address could keep `usize`; here the upstream View
64.   and the whole `FrameAddress`/`Inner` address algebra already work in `int`
65.   via `View::V = int`, so `int` is the consistent, cast-free choice.)
66. 
67. A wrapper struct (`KernelFrameView { addr: int }`) was considered and
68. **rejected** — see Rejected Alternatives.
69. 
70. ---
71. 
72. ## Well-formedness Invariant
73. 
74. `KernelFrame` currently has **no** `inv()`. Callers of `base()`
75. (`into_page_address`, and the page/stack address arithmetic behind it) rely on
76. the owned address being **page-aligned**. This is a caller-visible constraint
77. on the abstract state, so it belongs in `inv()`.
78. 
79. **Final decision (spec phase): single `inv()`, mirroring the verified sibling
80. `UserFrame::inv`.** The originally-sketched `internal_inv()` placeholder
81. (`pub closed spec fn internal_inv(&self) -> bool { true }`) was dropped: it would
82. be permanently `true` (the closed view `self@ == self.base@` already exposes the
83. alignment fact directly, so no implementation-consistency clause is needed), and
84. the `spec-design` skill discourages extra `pub spec fn`s on `impl MyType` beyond
85. `view`/`inv`. The result is identical in shape to `UserFrame`:
86. 
87. ```rust
88. impl KernelFrame {
89.     // Caller-visible well-formedness: the owned frame address is page-aligned.
90.     // Stated purely on the int view via the shared spec_page_size(); leaks no
91.     // implementation detail. Mirror of UserFrame::inv.
92.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
93.         self@ % spec_page_size() == 0
94.     }
95. }
96. ```
97. 
98. - `inv()` is **`pub open`** so callers can establish and consume it.
99. - `spec_page_size()` is the same `pub uninterp spec fn` already used by
100.   `FrameAddress::inv` (`self@ % spec_page_size() == 0`); reusing it keeps the
101.   alignment notion identical across the two types.
102. - No `internal_inv()` is defined; the alignment fact follows on the `new` /
103.   `base` paths directly from the required `base.inv()` / `self.inv()`.
104. 
105. No other `pub spec fn` is added to `impl KernelFrame` beyond `view` and `inv`.
106. 
107. ---
108. 
109. ## Spec Transition Functions
110. 
111. **There are none — and that is a deliberate, substitution-tested result.**
112. 
113. A `KernelFrame`'s abstract view is fixed at construction and **never changes**
114. for the lifetime of the handle. The in-scope API confirms this:
115. 
116. - `new(base)` is a **constructor**: it produces a fresh handle whose view *is*
117.   the input address. The contract is a constructor postcondition, not a
118.   transition on an existing view:
119. 
120.   ```rust
121.   // new (already external_body per tcb-allowed.md; keep its existing spec,
122.   // optionally surface the invariant it already guarantees):
123.   ensures match result {
124.       Ok(kf) => kf@ == base@ && kf.inv(),   // inv follows from required base.inv()
125.       Err(_) => true,                       // no ownership taken on failure
126.   }
127.   ```
128. 
129. - `base(&self)` is a **pure query** — no view change. Needed new spec:
130. 
131.   ```rust
132.   fn base(&self) -> (result: FrameAddress)
133.       requires self.inv(),
134.       ensures  result@ == self@ && result.inv();
135.   ```
136. 
137.   `result@ == self@` gives `kpage` the exact address; `result.inv()` (carried
138.   from `self.inv()`'s alignment clause) lets `into_page_address` and the stack
139.   arithmetic proceed.
140. 
141. - `drop(&mut self)` is a **destructor**. Its effect is *not* a transition on
142.   `KernelFrame`'s own view (the value is consumed). Dropping returns the frame
143.   `old(self)@` to the **global frame allocator**, so its postcondition is
144.   written against the allocator's View (`FrameAllocView` / `phys_view().frames`,
145.   the same View the manager already reasons over), e.g. "after drop,
146.   `old(self)@` is no longer allocated / is back in the free partition, and no
147.   other frame's status changes." Because that state lives in the allocator's
148.   abstraction, **no field is needed on `KernelFrameView` to express it**.
149. 
150. Consequently `impl KernelFrame`'s View needs no `spec_*` mutator helpers: the
151. view is immutable per handle, the only state change in the module
152. (allocation/free) is owned by the allocator's View.
153. 
154. ---
155. 
156. ## Design Rationale
157. 
158. ### Field: the view value `self@ : int` — the physical frame address
159. - **Why needed.** It is the one thing every caller reasons about: the manager
160.   proves the wrapped address equals the allocated address and builds
161.   `kernel_addr_set` / contiguity facts from it; `kpage` converts it to page and
162.   virtual addresses; `drop` frees *that* address. There is no caller use of
163.   `KernelFrame` that does not reduce to its address.
164. - **Substitution test.** *If `KernelFrame` were rewritten to store a raw
165.   `usize`, a frame number, or to compute the address on the fly instead of
166.   holding a `FrameAddress` — would "the physical frame address" still make
167.   sense?* **Yes.** Any owning-frame-handle implementation must denote *some*
168.   physical frame; its address is the implementation-independent identity of
169.   what is owned. ✅
170. - **Caller-only.** A caller understands "the physical address of the frame this
171.   handle owns" with zero knowledge of the internal field, the identity map, or
172.   page tables.
173. 
174. ### `inv()` clause: `self@ % spec_page_size() == 0` (page-aligned)
175. - **Why needed.** `base()` returns a `FrameAddress` that downstream code feeds
176.   to `into_page_address` and to `KernelStack` index arithmetic, both of which
177.   assume page alignment. Collecting this into `inv()` (instead of re-deriving it
178.   at every call site) follows the "missing wf()" anti-pattern fix.
179. - **Substitution test.** Alignment is a property of *what a physical frame is*
180.   (page-sized, page-aligned), not of how the handle stores it. Any
181.   implementation that owns a real frame yields a page-aligned address. ✅
182. - **Caller-abstract.** Stated purely on `self@` using the shared
183.   `spec_page_size()`; no implementation detail appears.
184. 
185. ### `internal_inv()` left as `true`
186. - Per methodology, implementation-consistency facts (here: "the stored
187.   `FrameAddress` satisfies its own `inv`") require seeing impl fields, so they
188.   are deferred to the spec phase. The caller-visible consequence (alignment) is
189.   already exposed through `inv()`.
190. 
191. ### Why no spec transition functions
192. - The handle's view is immutable; the only mutation in the module's lifecycle
193.   (a frame leaving the free partition on `new`'s upstream `alloc`, and returning
194.   on `drop`) is state of the **allocator**, captured by `FrameAllocView`, not by
195.   this per-object View. Modeling it here would duplicate (and risk
196.   desynchronizing) the allocator's abstraction.
197. 
198. ---
199. 
200. ## Rejected Alternatives
201. 
202. 1. **Wrapper struct `KernelFrameView { addr: int }`.**
203.    Rejected for minimality. A one-field struct adds a layer of `.addr`
204.    projections to every caller spec (`kf@.addr` vs `kf@`) and a `view()` that
205.    constructs the struct, with zero added information. `type V = int` is the
206.    simpler, already-adopted, caller-agreed abstraction. The `inv()` predicate
207.    lives perfectly well on `impl KernelFrame`.
208. 
209. 2. **Add an `allocated: bool` / ownership flag, or an allocator reference, to
210.    the View.**
211.    Rejected as an abstraction leak / wrong owner. Whether a frame is allocated
212.    is global allocator state, already modeled by `FrameAllocView`
213.    (`phys_view().frames`). The manager error path and `KernelStack::drop` reason
214.    about "freed exactly once" through the allocator's view, not through a flag
215.    on the handle. Duplicating it here would create two sources of truth that
216.    must be kept in sync. `drop`'s contract is therefore written against the
217.    allocator's View, leaving `KernelFrame`'s View minimal.

 # View Design: `mm::phys::kframe` (`KernelFrame`)
 
 ## Abstract Resource
 
 `KernelFrame` is an **owning handle to exactly one page-sized physical frame**.
 To the outside world it is a single value: *which physical frame this handle
 owns*. The only caller-observable abstract state is that frame's **physical
 address**. Everything else — the identity-mapping side effect, how the address
 is stored, the page-table mechanics, the byte contents reachable through
 `Deref` — is internal or out of scope.
 
 In-scope functions: `KernelFrame::new` (constructor), `KernelFrame::base`
 (query), `KernelFrame::drop` (destructor).
 
 ---
 
 ## Inherited View (from upstream `mm::phys` manager verification)
 
 ```rust
 impl View for KernelFrame {
     type V = int;
     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int { self.base@ }   // physical frame address
 }
 ```
 
 This View was added when the manager layer (`alloc_kernel_frame`,
 `alloc_many_kernel_frames`) was verified top-down. It is treated here as an
 **input to evaluate**, not a finished design.
 
 ### Evaluation against *all* callers
 
 | Caller | Uses `self@` as… | Verdict |
 |---|---|---|
 | `manager::alloc_kernel_frame` | the allocated address: `kf@ == frame_addr@`, `lemma_kernel_alloc_one(..., result->Ok_0@)` | ✅ address |
 | `manager::alloc_many_kernel_frames` | `kernel_frames_contiguous`, `kernel_addr_set(frames@)` — set/sequence of owned addresses | ✅ address |
 | `virt::kpage::KernelPage::base` | `kframe.base().into_page_address().into_virtual_address()` — needs the address + page-alignment | ✅ address |
 | `virt::kpage::KernelPage::frame_address` | returns `kframe.base()` verbatim | ✅ address |
 | `Drop` sites (manager error path, `KernelStack::drop`) | identity of the frame being freed exactly once | ✅ address |
 
 Every caller agrees: the abstract state is the **physical frame address**, an
 `int`. No caller needs anything else.
 
 **Decision: KEEP `type V = int` unchanged.** It already passes the
 substitution test from every caller's perspective (see Rationale). Nothing is
 renamed, added, or removed. The View definition is left exactly as inherited.
 
 ---
 
 ## View Struct
 
 The View is a primitive, not a struct:
 
 ```rust
 impl View for KernelFrame {
     type V = int;                       // the physical address of the owned frame
     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int { /* maps impl field -> address */ }
 }
 ```
 
 - `view()` stays **`closed`**: public so callers write `kf@`, closed so the
   field-level mapping (currently `self.base@`) does not leak.
 - The value space is `int` — the mathematical physical address. (Per the
   view-design exception, an address could keep `usize`; here the upstream View
   and the whole `FrameAddress`/`Inner` address algebra already work in `int`
   via `View::V = int`, so `int` is the consistent, cast-free choice.)
 
 A wrapper struct (`KernelFrameView { addr: int }`) was considered and
 **rejected** — see Rejected Alternatives.
 
 ---
 
 ## Well-formedness Invariant
 
 `KernelFrame` currently has **no** `inv()`. Callers of `base()`
 (`into_page_address`, and the page/stack address arithmetic behind it) rely on
 the owned address being **page-aligned**. This is a caller-visible constraint
 on the abstract state, so it belongs in `inv()`.
 
 **Final decision (spec phase): single `inv()`, mirroring the verified sibling
 `UserFrame::inv`.** The originally-sketched `internal_inv()` placeholder
 (`pub closed spec fn internal_inv(&self) -> bool { true }`) was dropped: it would
 be permanently `true` (the closed view `self@ == self.base@` already exposes the
 alignment fact directly, so no implementation-consistency clause is needed), and
 the `spec-design` skill discourages extra `pub spec fn`s on `impl MyType` beyond
 `view`/`inv`. The result is identical in shape to `UserFrame`:
 
 ```rust
 impl KernelFrame {
     // Caller-visible well-formedness: the owned frame address is page-aligned.
     // Stated purely on the int view via the shared spec_page_size(); leaks no
     // implementation detail. Mirror of UserFrame::inv.
     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
         self@ % spec_page_size() == 0
     }
 }
 ```
 
 - `inv()` is **`pub open`** so callers can establish and consume it.
 - `spec_page_size()` is the same `pub uninterp spec fn` already used by
   `FrameAddress::inv` (`self@ % spec_page_size() == 0`); reusing it keeps the
   alignment notion identical across the two types.
 - No `internal_inv()` is defined; the alignment fact follows on the `new` /
   `base` paths directly from the required `base.inv()` / `self.inv()`.
 
 No other `pub spec fn` is added to `impl KernelFrame` beyond `view` and `inv`.
 
 ---
 
 ## Spec Transition Functions
 
 **There are none — and that is a deliberate, substitution-tested result.**
 
 A `KernelFrame`'s abstract view is fixed at construction and **never changes**
 for the lifetime of the handle. The in-scope API confirms this:
 
 - `new(base)` is a **constructor**: it produces a fresh handle whose view *is*
   the input address. The contract is a constructor postcondition, not a
   transition on an existing view:
 
   ```rust
   // new (already external_body per tcb-allowed.md; keep its existing spec,
   // optionally surface the invariant it already guarantees):
   ensures match result {
       Ok(kf) => kf@ == base@ && kf.inv(),   // inv follows from required base.inv()
       Err(_) => true,                       // no ownership taken on failure
   }
   ```
 
 - `base(&self)` is a **pure query** — no view change. Needed new spec:
 
   ```rust
   fn base(&self) -> (result: FrameAddress)
       requires self.inv(),
       ensures  result@ == self@ && result.inv();
   ```
 
   `result@ == self@` gives `kpage` the exact address; `result.inv()` (carried
   from `self.inv()`'s alignment clause) lets `into_page_address` and the stack
   arithmetic proceed.
 
 - `drop(&mut self)` is a **destructor**. Its effect is *not* a transition on
   `KernelFrame`'s own view (the value is consumed). Dropping returns the frame
   `old(self)@` to the **global frame allocator**, so its postcondition is
   written against the allocator's View (`FrameAllocView` / `phys_view().frames`,
   the same View the manager already reasons over), e.g. "after drop,
   `old(self)@` is no longer allocated / is back in the free partition, and no
   other frame's status changes." Because that state lives in the allocator's
   abstraction, **no field is needed on `KernelFrameView` to express it**.
 
 Consequently `impl KernelFrame`'s View needs no `spec_*` mutator helpers: the
 view is immutable per handle, the only state change in the module
 (allocation/free) is owned by the allocator's View.
 
 ---
 
 ## Design Rationale
 
 ### Field: the view value `self@ : int` — the physical frame address
 - **Why needed.** It is the one thing every caller reasons about: the manager
   proves the wrapped address equals the allocated address and builds
   `kernel_addr_set` / contiguity facts from it; `kpage` converts it to page and
   virtual addresses; `drop` frees *that* address. There is no caller use of
   `KernelFrame` that does not reduce to its address.
 - **Substitution test.** *If `KernelFrame` were rewritten to store a raw
   `usize`, a frame number, or to compute the address on the fly instead of
   holding a `FrameAddress` — would "the physical frame address" still make
   sense?* **Yes.** Any owning-frame-handle implementation must denote *some*
   physical frame; its address is the implementation-independent identity of
   what is owned. ✅
 - **Caller-only.** A caller understands "the physical address of the frame this
   handle owns" with zero knowledge of the internal field, the identity map, or
   page tables.
 
 ### `inv()` clause: `self@ % spec_page_size() == 0` (page-aligned)
 - **Why needed.** `base()` returns a `FrameAddress` that downstream code feeds
   to `into_page_address` and to `KernelStack` index arithmetic, both of which
   assume page alignment. Collecting this into `inv()` (instead of re-deriving it
   at every call site) follows the "missing wf()" anti-pattern fix.
 - **Substitution test.** Alignment is a property of *what a physical frame is*
   (page-sized, page-aligned), not of how the handle stores it. Any
   implementation that owns a real frame yields a page-aligned address. ✅
 - **Caller-abstract.** Stated purely on `self@` using the shared
   `spec_page_size()`; no implementation detail appears.
 
 ### `internal_inv()` left as `true`
 - Per methodology, implementation-consistency facts (here: "the stored
   `FrameAddress` satisfies its own `inv`") require seeing impl fields, so they
   are deferred to the spec phase. The caller-visible consequence (alignment) is
   already exposed through `inv()`.
 
 ### Why no spec transition functions
 - The handle's view is immutable; the only mutation in the module's lifecycle
   (a frame leaving the free partition on `new`'s upstream `alloc`, and returning
   on `drop`) is state of the **allocator**, captured by `FrameAllocView`, not by
   this per-object View. Modeling it here would duplicate (and risk
   desynchronizing) the allocator's abstraction.
 
 ---
 
 ## Rejected Alternatives
 
 1. **Wrapper struct `KernelFrameView { addr: int }`.**
    Rejected for minimality. A one-field struct adds a layer of `.addr`
    projections to every caller spec (`kf@.addr` vs `kf@`) and a `view()` that
    constructs the struct, with zero added information. `type V = int` is the
    simpler, already-adopted, caller-agreed abstraction. The `inv()` predicate
    lives perfectly well on `impl KernelFrame`.
 
 2. **Add an `allocated: bool` / ownership flag, or an allocator reference, to
    the View.**
    Rejected as an abstraction leak / wrong owner. Whether a frame is allocated
    is global allocator state, already modeled by `FrameAllocView`
    (`phys_view().frames`). The manager error path and `KernelStack::drop` reason
    about "freed exactly once" through the allocator's view, not through a flag
    on the handle. Duplicating it here would create two sources of truth that
    must be kept in sync. `drop`'s contract is therefore written against the
    allocator's View, leaving `KernelFrame`'s View minimal.
 
 3. **Add a `mapped: bool` (identity-mapping) field.**
    Rejected. The caller analysis is explicit: callers *do not care* about the
    identity-mapping side effect of `new`. It is an internal effect of
    `mm::virt::identity_map_page` (outside `mm::phys` scope) and observable to no
    in-scope caller. Including it would leak HOW the handle is set up.
 
 4. **Add the frame's byte contents (e.g. `Seq<u8>` / a `PointsTo`) to the
    View.**
    Rejected for this scope. Byte contents are only relevant to `Deref`,
    `DerefMut`, and `clear` — all explicitly **out of scope** and not to be
    touched. The in-scope functions (`new`, `base`, `drop`) concern only frame
    *ownership/identity*, i.e. the address. If/when the access functions are
    verified, the natural model for their bytes is a `PointsTo` over the
    identity-mapped region (keyed by `self@`), not a field baked into this
    ownership View — so adding it now would be premature and would destabilize
    the View the current callers already depend on.
 
 5. **Change `view()` to `usize` instead of `int`.**
    Rejected for consistency. The entire surrounding address algebra
    (`FrameAddress`, `Inner`, `FrameAllocView`, the manager's
    `kernel_addr_set`/contiguity lemmas) is expressed with `View::V = int`.
    Switching this one View to `usize` would force casts at every interface with
    those specs for no benefit; the inherited `int` view is correct as-is.
 
 6. **Strengthen `new`'s `Err(_) => true` into an explicit "frame not consumed"
    postcondition.**
    Considered (the caller does rely on `new` not freeing `base` on failure), but
    **out of scope for View design** and partly outside this module: the
    no-consume guarantee on the error path is currently provided by `new` being a
    trusted `external_body` dependency contract (it never touches the global
    allocator on `Err`) plus the caller's explicit `frame::free(base)` cleanup.
    The View needs no field to express it. Noted here for the spec phase; the
    View design is unaffected.
 
 ---
 
 ## Quality Review
 
 | Criterion | Check |
 |---|---|
 | **Substitution** | The address (and its page-alignment) survive any rewrite of how the handle stores/derives the frame. ✅ |
 | **Caller-only** | Every caller reads `kf@` as "the owned frame's physical address" with no impl knowledge. ✅ |
 | **Complete** | All in-scope caller-observable concepts — owned-frame identity (`new`/`base`/`drop`), set/contiguity facts, page-aligned conversions — are expressible from `self@` + `inv()`. Allocator/ownership effects of `drop` are covered by the existing allocator View. ✅ |
 | **Minimal** | Single `int` view; the one `inv()` clause is used by every `base()` caller. No unused fields. ✅ |
 | **No code-as-spec** | The View states *what* (a physical address, page-aligned), never *how* (identity map, page tables, field layout). ✅ |

37. /// A type that represents a kernel frame.
38. #[derive(Debug)]
39. #[verus_verify(external_derive)]
40. pub struct KernelFrame {
41.     /// Frame address.

43. }

51.
