59. // Dependency contract for the manager layer: wrapping a `FrameAddress` produces a handle whose
60. // abstract address is the same physical frame.
61. #[verus_verify]
62. impl KernelFrame {
63.     ///
64.     /// # Description
65.     ///
66.     /// Instantiates a kernel frame.
67.     ///
68.     /// # Parameters
69.     ///
70.     /// - `base`: Frame address.
71.     ///
72.     /// # Returns
73.     ///
74.     /// Upon success, a kernel frame is returned. Upon failure, an error is returned instead.
75.     ///
76.     // Dependency contract: wrapping a frame goes through `mm::virt::identity_map_page`, which
77.     // is outside the verification scope of `mm::phys`. On success the returned handle owns the
78.     // same physical frame that was passed in. `external_body` per `verus-ai-logs/tcb-allowed.md`:
79.     // the identity-mapping side effect lives in `mm::virt` and the body's `?`/log closures call
80.     // into that layer, so the wrap contract is trusted until `mm::virt` is verified.
81.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
82.     #[verus_spec(result =>
83.         requires
84.             base.inv(),
85.         ensures
86.             match result {
87.                 Ok(kf) => {
88.                     &&& kf@ == base@
89.                     &&& kf.inv()
90.                 },
91.                 Err(_) => true,
92.             },
93.     )]
94.     pub(super) fn new(base: FrameAddress) -> Result<Self, Error> {
95.         // Ensure the frame is identity-mapped in the kernel address space so that
96.         // Deref/DerefMut can safely access it. This lazily installs a page
97.         // table entry if needed (page tables come from a BSS pool, so no recursive frame
98.         // allocation occurs).
99.         let phys_addr: PageAligned<PhysicalAddress> =
100.             PageAligned::from_raw_value(base.into_raw_value()).map_err(|e| {
101.                 error!("frame base is not page-aligned: {e:?}");
102.                 e
103.             })?;
104.         crate::mm::virt::identity_map_page(phys_addr).map_err(|e| {
105.             error!("failed to identity-map frame: {:?}", e);
106.             e
107.         })?;
108. 
109.         Ok(Self { base })
110.     }
111. }

114. impl KernelFrame {
115. 
116.     ///
117.     /// # Description
118.     ///
119.     /// Returns the base address of the target kernel frame.
120.     ///
121.     /// # Returns
122.     ///
123.     /// The base address of the target kernel frame.
124.     ///
125.     // Pure accessor: returns the owned frame's physical address unchanged. `result@ == self@`
126.     // gives `kpage` the exact address; `result.inv()` (page alignment carried from `self.inv()`)
127.     // lets `into_page_address` and the `KernelStack` arithmetic behind it proceed.
128.     #[verus_spec(result =>
129.         requires
130.             self.inv(),
131.         ensures
132.             result@ == self@,
133.             result.inv(),
134.     )]

137.     }

140. impl KernelFrame {
141. 
142.     ///
143.     /// # Description
144.     ///
145.     /// Clears the target kernel frame.
146.     ///
147.     /// Uses the identity-map `memset` backend so that the write runs in the kernel address space.
148.     /// This avoids a page fault when the current CR3 points to a user page directory that lacks
149.     /// the PDE for this frame's physical address.
150.     ///
151.     pub fn clear(&mut self) -> Result<(), Error> {
152.         let base: *mut u8 = self.base.into_raw_value() as *mut u8;
153.         crate::mm::virt::memset(base, 0, mem::PAGE_SIZE).map_err(|e| {
154.             error!("memset failed: {:?}", e);
155.             e
156.         })
157.     }
158. }
159. 
160. /// # Safety
161. ///
162. /// `Deref` accesses the identity-mapped frame directly. The caller must ensure that the current
163. /// CR3 points to a page directory that has the relevant PDE for this frame's physical address
164. /// (i.e., the kernel page directory, or a user page directory into which the PDE has been
165. /// propagated via [`sync_kernel_pdes`](crate::mm::virt::sync_kernel_pdes)). For CR3-agnostic
166. /// writes, prefer [`KernelFrame::clear()`] which uses the identity-map `memset` backend.
167. impl Deref for KernelFrame {
168.     type Target = [u8];
169. 
170.     fn deref(&self) -> &Self::Target {
171.         let ptr: usize = self.base.into_raw_value();
172.         unsafe { core::slice::from_raw_parts(ptr as *const u8, mem::PAGE_SIZE) }
173.     }
174. }
175. 
176. /// # Safety
177. ///
178. /// See [`Deref`] impl — the same CR3 invariant applies.
179. impl DerefMut for KernelFrame {
180.     fn deref_mut(&mut self) -> &mut Self::Target {
181.         let ptr: usize = self.base.into_raw_value();
182.         unsafe { core::slice::from_raw_parts_mut(ptr as *mut u8, mem::PAGE_SIZE) }
183.     }
184. }

187. impl Drop for KernelFrame {
188.     // Releasing the handle returns its physical frame to the global frame allocator via
189.     // `super::frame::free`, which is best-effort (`ensures true`) and `opens_invariants none`/
190.     // `no_unwind`, so `drop` makes no abstract postcondition. Callers (the manager error path,
191.     // `KernelStack::drop`) rely on this being the sole, complete deallocation step. Mirror of
192.     // `UserFrame::drop`.
193.     #[verus_spec(
194.         opens_invariants none
195.         no_unwind
196.     )]
197.     fn drop(&mut self) {
198.         if let Err(e) = super::frame::free(self.base) {
199.             #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
200.             error!("failed to free kernel frame: {:?}", e);
201.         }
202.     }
203. }

data.deltaContent: I
'm noticing that UserFrame::new is implemented inline with just a
simple struct initialization, while KernelFrame::new is marked as external_body because it calls identity_map_page. Both
follow the same drop pattern though, which is reassuring. The key difference is in
their views—UserFrame uses FrameAllocView while KernelFrame uses int—and according
to the design docs, this relates to how the mirror pattern handles the invariant shape,
though the thought seems to cut off there.
Looking
at the drop implementation, the actual free call executes in both builds without
any cfg gate, while only the error logging is gated behind the verus_keep_ghost flag
. The control flow stays identical, so this is purely a logging concern.
In the verus build, the error variable gets bound but unused, which mirrors the same
pattern in UserFrame, and since that module verifies cleanly, there's no issue

here.

For the spec quality, new requires base.inv() for page alignment and ensures either success
with the frame matching the base and maintaining invariants, or failure with a
trivial postcondition. It's marked external_body in the TCB,
which is allowed. The weak Err postcondition is justified since the external function is trusted not to consume the base on
error, leaving cleanup to the caller—acceptable but worth noting.
The
base accessor is straightforward: requires self.inv() and ensures the result equals

self with invariants preserved.

The drop function has no abstract postcondition, which
means the actual freeing effect isn't captured in the spec. Both caller analysis and view design note that callers depend
on drop freeing exactly once, but that's allocator state that can't be expressed without the
allocator view in scope. Since frame::free itself has no abstract postcondition either, this is a spec-completeness gap consistent with the layering design

—acceptable given the constraints.

For caller expectations, new covers the
page-alignment requirement and the Ok case where the frame matches the base,
but the Err case relies on external_body trust plus manual caller cleanup rather than a direct
spec guarantee. That's the one weak point in coverage.

data.reasoningText:
I'm noticing that UserFrame::new is implemented inline with just a simple struct initialization, while KernelFrame::new is marked as external_body because it calls identity_map_page. Both follow the same drop pattern though, which is reassuring. The key difference is in their views—UserFrame uses FrameAllocView while KernelFrame uses int—and according to the design docs, this relates to how the mirror pattern handles the invariant shape, though the thought seems to cut off there.

Looking at the drop implementation, the actual free call executes in both builds without any cfg gate, while only the error logging is gated behind the verus_keep_ghost flag. The control flow stays identical, so this is purely a logging concern. In the verus build, the error variable gets bound but unused, which mirrors the same pattern in UserFrame, and since that module verifies cleanly, there's no issue here.

For the spec quality, new requires base.inv() for page alignment and ensures either success with the frame matching the base and maintaining invariants, or failure with a trivial postcondition. It's marked external_body in the TCB, which is allowed. The weak Err postcondition is justified since the external function is trusted not to consume the base on error, leaving cleanup to the caller—acceptable but worth noting.

The base accessor is straightforward: requires self.inv() and ensures the result equals self with invariants preserved.

The drop function has no abstract postcondition, which means the actual freeing effect isn't captured in the spec. Both caller analysis and view design note that callers depend on drop freeing exactly once, but that's allocator state that can't be expressed without the allocator view in scope. Since frame::free itself has no abstract postcondition either, this is a spec-completeness gap consistent with the layering design—acceptable given the constraints.

For caller expectations, new covers the page-alignment requirement and the Ok case where the frame matches the base, but the Err case relies on external_body trust plus manual caller cleanup rather than a direct spec guarantee. That's the one weak point in coverage. So that's 5 fully covered expectations from the spec, with 2 deferred trust items (the Err non-consumption and drop's single-free guarantee). The build-hygiene bug with the duplicate import is confirmed fixed — only one prelude import remains in kframe.rs. No correctness bugs exist; the duplicate import was the only real defect and it's resolved. Verifying the external_body usage: it's the sole instance in kframe, it's listed in tcb-allowed.md, and there are no admit/assume statements or VERUS REWRITE comments polluting the code.

Everything checks out — time to write the review.

# Final Independent Review — `mm::phys::kframe`

Reviewer: Claude (independent, from-scratch static analysis)
Date: 2026-06-15
Scope: in-scope functions only — `KernelFrame::new`, `KernelFrame::base`, `KernelFrame::drop`.
Out of scope (not flagged): `clear`, `deref`, `deref_mut`, and all sibling modules.
Method: grep/view over `kframe.rs`, `kframe.spec.rs`, `kframe.proof.rs`; static read of
`cheating-detail.txt`; cross-check of `tcb-allowed.md`, `caller_analysis.md`, `view_design.md`,
`bugs.md`. `make verify-kernel` was NOT re-run (per instructions; claim verified statically).

---

## Spec Quality

**`KernelFrame::new`** (`kframe.rs:81-110`, `external_body`)
- `requires base.inv()` — page-alignment precondition on the input frame address. Real, caller-met
  constraint (addresses come from `frame::alloc`/`alloc_contiguous`). ✅
- `ensures Ok(kf) => kf@ == base@ && kf.inv()` — preserves frame identity (the manager's
  `lemma_kernel_alloc_one` needs `kf@ == frame_addr@`) and re-exposes page-alignment for `base()`

151.    or describing computation step-by-step. Bad: recursive quicksort in
152.    spec. Good: `is_sorted(result@) && is_permutation_of(result@, input@)`.
153. 5. **One-Sided Error Spec** — only specifies success, says nothing
154.    (or `true`) about failure. Error paths need equal rigor.
155. 6. **Missing Frame Condition / Field-by-Field Conjunction** — ensures says
156.    what changed but not what didn't, OR lists unchanged fields one by one
157.    (fragile — easy to forget a field). **Always use struct update syntax**
158.    (`..old(self)@`) so completeness is guaranteed by construction:
159. 
160.    Bad (fragile — silent field omission):
161.    ```
162.    self@.field_a == old(self)@.field_a,
163.    self@.field_b == old(self)@.field_b,
164.    self@.field_c == new_value,
165.    // forgot field_d — spec is incomplete!
166.    ```
167.    Good (complete by construction):
168.    ```
169.    self@ == ViewType { field_c: new_value, ..old(self)@ }
170.    ```
171.    This applies everywhere state changes appear in ensures — whether
172.    inline or via spec transition functions.
173. 7. **Separate Ok/Err Conditions** — using `result.is_ok() ==> ...` and
174.    `result.is_err() ==> ...` as separate ensures clauses instead of a
175.    single `match`. The `match` form is complete by construction and
176.    prevents accidentally omitting one arm:
177. 
178.    Bad:
179.    ```
180.    ensures
181.        result.is_ok() ==> /* success postcondition */,
182.        result.is_err() ==> self@ == old(self)@,
183.    ```
184.    Good:
185.    ```
186.    ensures match result {
187.        Ok(v)  => /* success postcondition */,
188.        Err(e) => self@ == old(self)@,
189.    }
190.    ```
191. 8. **Tautological Postconditions** — trivially true for any return value.
192. 9. **Subsumed Properties** — logically implied by a stronger property
193.    already present. Before adding an ensures clause, check: is this
194.    derivable from `self.inv()` combined with the other ensures? If so,
195.    delete it — redundant clauses obscure the spec's intent and make
196.    reviews harder.
197. 10. **Over-specification** — forcing a particular implementation strategy.
198.    Only add specificity when callers genuinely depend on it.
199. 11. **Scattered Invariant** — the same property appears in `requires` of
200.     every (or nearly every) method. A universally required property is an
201.     invariant — move it to `inv()` and maintain it in `ensures`.

203.     avoid writing a concrete spec definition, then injecting properties
204.     via `external_body` proof axioms. This combination is equivalent to
205.     `assume` — it introduces unverified assumptions about a function

217. Every function that can fail should specify **what happens on failure**
218. with the same rigor as the success path.

221. 2. **Bidirectional Failure Condition** — express error conditions as abstract
222.    predicates on the module's interface state, not as a list of individual
223.    code checks. Ask: what condition at the interface level makes success
224.    impossible?

226.    possible, the spec must guarantee success (i.e., the function must

228.    even when success is achievable is under-specified — callers cannot
229.    rely on it. Use `match` on the return value to specify both arms:

242. - **Display/formatting** — debug output, logging, string representation
243. - **Boilerplate trait impls** — derived traits, mechanical delegations
